Seminar Title:

Molecular mechanism of non-host defence mediated by active protagonists conferring broad-spectrum disease resistance against rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae) by programmed cell death

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Life Science

Speaker Name:

Reecha Mohapatra ( Rollno : 520ls2005)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

LS Seminar Hall

Date and Time:

12 Oct 2026 10:00AM

Contact:

Binod Bihari Sahu

Abstract:

Non-host resistance (NHR) is an effective, broad-spectrum form of resistance that prevents pathogen invasion in non-hosts, but how defence metabolism is integrated with transcriptional, redox, and cellular immune responses to achieve pathogen resistance is enigmatic. We examined the structural, evolutionary, metabolic, and cellular roles of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase 2 (MTHFR2) in Arabidopsis thaliana NHR against the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (M. oryzae). We defined MTHFR2 as a component of a multifaceted NHR network using a combination of genetic and infection assays, untargeted LC-HRMS metabolomics, transcriptional and cytochemical analysis, live-cell imaging, in vitro antifungal assays, and molecular modelling. Loss of MTHFR2 caused prominent changes in one-carbon and sulfur metabolism, with severe depletion of methionine- and cysteine-derived metabolites, including &gt290-fold reduction in glucoraphanin, and was associated with perturbation of salicylic acid-related signalling and cellular redox status. Additional genetic interaction analysis revealed that simultaneous loss of MTHFR2 and PEN2, or the receptor-like kinase SOBIR1, severely degraded NHR, which resulted in accelerated fungal penetration and hyphal growth disrupting the host immune system. Structural study of the EMS-derived MTHFR2 A55V variation uncovered the molecular basis for this phenotype, with the active site being perturbed and conformational instability enhanced, despite the overall architecture of the protein being largely preserved. The mutant exhibited a slight reduction in Ramachandran-favoured conformations (94.097% versus 94.662% in the wild type), a 48.7% increase in structural deviation, and an 183% increase in conformational variability, while residues within the NADH-binding pocket exhibited 39.8% increase in flexibility consistent with impaired ligand recognition and altered 5-CH3-THF production. Evolutionary research indicated that MTHFR2 is highly conserved in numerous plant species, and the soybean ortholog shows high sequence similarity, which supports the retention of its metabolic function during plant evolution. Consequently, extracts from soybeans decreased M. oryzae conidial germination and development, suggesting that MTHFR2-associated metabolic defence may be part of a larger metabolite-based resistance mechanism. At the cellular level, MTHFR2-dependent metabolic competence was coupled with transcriptional rewiring, ROS signalling, structural reinforcement, and regulated cell-death responses. Effective NHR was characterized by spatially confined ROS buildup and localized callose and lignin deposition at invasion sites, while disruption of MTHFR2, PEN2, or RBOHF led to widespread or dysregulated defence responses. Transcriptional analyses indicated compensatory activation of MPK3&ndashWRKY signalling and MYB&ndashCYP-dependent indolic secondary-metabolite pathways, including CYP79B2, CYP79B3, and CYP83B1. In the pen2/mthfr2/rbohf background, these compensatory responses were not sufficient to contain the pathogen and were associated with extensive fungal invasion and branching, membrane damage, altered endocytic trafficking, impaired cellular viability, and disrupted chloroplast organization. Altered autophagy-related mechanisms and localized cell death responses further connected metabolic and redox disturbances to cellular containment of fungal invasion. To summarize, our findings identify MTHFR2 as a conserved metabolic hub linking reprogramming of one-carbon and sulfur metabolism to transcriptional rewiring, ROS signalling, cell-wall reinforcement, and hypersensitive/autophagy-associated cell death pathways. These integrated defence layers constitute a spatially coordinated continuum that allows Arabidopsis to constrain M. oryzae invasion and offers a molecular rationale for the integration of conserved metabolic activities into broad-spectrum NHR.
